analysis.one_liner: Guarantees patients in managed care direct access to emergency and specialty care, specialists, and outside appeals of coverage denials.
analysis.headline: The Patients' Bill of Rights Act was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action in the 105th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set a floor of protections for people in employer and other group health plans: emergency room visits covered without prior approval and at in-network cost, direct access to obstetricians and standing referrals to specialists, outside review when a plan denies care, protection for doctors who speak up about quality problems, minimum hospital stays after breast cancer surgery, and coverage of clinical trials. It never advanced beyond its first day in the Senate: it was read twice and sent to the Finance Committee, where it stayed until Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 160 million Americans with job-based or other private health coverage at the time, especially patients in HMOs and managed care plans. The bill would have helped people who face coverage denials, women needing gynecological and breast cancer care, patients with serious illnesses seeking specialists or clinical trials, and doctors whose medical judgment insurers had been overriding. Patients would have gained the right to take a coverage dispute to an independent outside reviewer instead of depending on the insurer's own decision.

how_it_helps.text: Requires plans to cover emergency services without prior authorization and to hold patients to in-network costs even when the hospital is out of network [S2] [S3].
Lets women designate an obstetrician-gynecologist as their primary care provider and see one for routine gynecological care without a referral [S2].
Requires plans to provide standing referrals to specialists for people with ongoing serious conditions and direct access to a specialist as primary coordinator of care [S2].
Creates a binding external appeals process for coverage denials that jeopardize a patient's health, paid for by the insurer [S2] [S3].
Bans insurer contracts that gag doctors from discussing treatment options with patients and bars financial incentives rewarding reviewers for denying care [S2].

Sets minimum 48-hour hospital stays after mastectomy and 24 hours after lymph node dissection, with the treating physician able to approve earlier discharge only in consultation with the patient [S2].
Requires coverage of routine patient costs for patients in approved NIH, VA, or Defense Department clinical trials [S2] [S3].
Protects health care workers from retaliation for reporting quality problems to regulators and protects patients from retaliation for filing grievances [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care companies would bear the direct cost: they would have to cover emergency and specialist care more broadly, pay for external reviews, and limit incentives that reward denial of care. Employers sponsoring plans would face some of the pass-through of higher premiums, though the bill states employers are not required to pay additional costs for point-of-service options [S2].

drawbacks.text: Mandated benefits and external review requirements raise premiums; the employer-financed system meant some of that cost would show up in wages or in employers dropping coverage. The bill itself acknowledges plans may charge higher premiums for out-of-network point-of-service options [S2].

The bill lets plans impose higher premiums and cost-sharing on patients who choose out-of-network point-of-service coverage, so some of the 'choice' it guarantees comes at the patient's own expense [S3].

It requires choice among providers but does not guarantee that the specific provider a patient wants will be in the network; plans can still limit networks and satisfy the bill by simply offering information [S2] [S3].
External appeals were limited to cases above a monetary threshold or where health is jeopardized, leaving many routine denials outside the process [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing denials, narrow networks, and drive-through care, the protections were substantial and targeted at well-documented problems of the managed care era. The cost — higher premiums passed to employers and workers — was real but modest compared with the stakes for people whose insurer denied needed care. The bill was a rights-and-appeals framework rather than a coverage expansion, so it did not address the uninsured.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill on March 31, 1998, read it twice, sent it to the Finance Committee, and never took it up again before the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Daschle and 21 Democratic colleagues introduced the Patients' Bill of Rights Act in the Senate on March 31, 1998 [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance; no further action appears in the record for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
It accumulated 31 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a hearing referral outcome in the Senate [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care companies were better off: none of the coverage mandates, appeal rights, or restrictions on denial incentives took effect. Patients in managed care plans continued to face coverage denials without the outside review this bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and managed care companies

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Patients' Bill of Rights Act on March 31, 1998 [S1] [S5].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a markup, hearing, or vote from March 31, 1998 until the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Republican Senate leadership
against.role: Majority leadership, controlled the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought a Patients' Bill of Rights to a Senate vote; the 105th Congress ended without floor action on this bill.

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed managed care regulation and lobbied against patient bill of rights mandates during the 1998 debate.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill came from the Democratic leadership; no Republican support appears in the record [S4].

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care companies
industries.note: The bill would have mandated broader coverage of emergency and specialist care, required independent external appeals of denials, and barred financial incentives that reward reviewers for rejecting care. Its interests ran against the patient protections in the bill.
Mandated benefits and review requirements would raise the cost of employer coverage. The bill shields employers from some direct cost obligations but would still face higher premiums.

Doctors would regain authority over medical decisions, gain protection from insurer gag clauses and retaliation for advocating for patients, and get guaranteed reimbursement for extended transitional care.
